chapter: Technique and the Covington band's sound
title: Three-string versus four-string bass, bass horn and the jitney dance
summary: Zardis explains why a three-string bass hampered reading music, mentions playing bass horn and a jitney dance with Petit.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well I'll tell you, I bought a bass with the same bass I tell you about with the old man. Well he had three strings on that bass. Bill and Moran. Yeah, Bill and Moran. Well after that third, that fourth string, I go to make a G, like sometimes I'm playing a soft number and I have my bow and I will make a low G, you know what I mean? Well I couldn't make my low G. Sometimes I have to finger my G down from this F, you see? And if I didn't finger that G I'd have to make that open G. What I mean by making a G open all the time when it don't sound, you know what I mean? This don't sound right. See because you take music now, if you're reading music, like I used to read the whole other music, and you can't play the three string bass with them dots. You know if you're reading you can't do that. I played a little horn too. I played bass horn too. But I was playing that E flat. I played bass horn. Well not so long. I liked the round here. And the same bar there loved me a whole lot. George. And I said well I didn't like it. I didn't like it. I wake up here at what they say, I played Buddy Petite there, up at St. Charles and Pardis. There used to be a Jitney dance. You know the Jitney dance? That's a dying dance. Yeah. I remember the old Fern and Budweiser. Yeah, yeah. Well that's right. Well I waited up there with Buddy playing that Jitney dance a long time, just playing the horn. I used to have a pretty horn. I had blue lights, green lights, and red lights. When one light go on, they don't want to come on, you know. It won't go off. Yeah, I've seen those.
